A numeral at a type of a program's own that declares no coercion from the
numeral's type is not converted into its default and then coerced, since
coercion does not chain (below); it is a static error.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 made coercion
the only conversion of a value at a place of another type, and excluded a place
whose declared type is a supertype of the type converted to.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral where nothing fixes a
type is converted into its default; the default is a rule beside coercion, and
the paragraph above stands as it was.
It decided on 9~November 2026 that a numeral's coercion into a type is the one
that the type declares from the numeral's type, generic over the numeral's four
numbers (\secref{literals}), for the number types of \library\ as for a type of
a program's own.}

Coercion from \VAR{T} to \VAR{U} may occur in an expression context
where the context expects the expression to have type \VAR{U} and
the type of the expression is a subtype of \VAR{T} except for the following
cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item type ascriptions (see \secref{type-ascription})
\item type assumptions (see \secref{type-assumption})
\end{itemize}
For example, a coercion may occur in a variable definition when the
type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and keeps its result for the place; it refuses a numeral
only when the place is evaluated: one outside an integer type's range, one
that rounds to an infinity of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, one at a
type that declares no coercion from the numeral's type or whose coercion's
\KWD{where} clause the numeral does not meet, a negated numeral at a type
without a prefix \EXP{-}, a folded constant at a type of a program's own
without a coercion from the constant's default type, and a numeral bound to a
variable declared of a numeral type.
It refuses when it loads a program a numeral type written as a type that an
object or a trait extends, or as a static argument.
It converts a
numeral at a parameter of the declaration that a call chooses, at a variable or
a field of a declared type and at a declared return type, but not one passed
through a tuple or a varargs parameter (rows~395 and~511).
The compiled type checker does not apply the rule that a numeral type is written
only as a parameter type to the libraries' own files.
A numeral type declares no \EXP{=} with a number type, so a numeral compared by
\EXP{=} with a number of a type that declares no \EXP{=} with the numeral's
default type meets the top-level \EXP{=} of \library, whose parameters are of
type \TYP{Any} and which takes the numeral at its default: the interpreter answers \EXP{u = 0} \VAR{false}, and
\EXP{u \neq 0} \VAR{true}, for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, none of which declares \EXP{=} with
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (rows~966 and~973 of the revival's gap ledger; the
expected failure \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss}
asserts \VAR{true}), and whether \EXP{u = 0} is \VAR{true} is open; the compiled
path's own library declares no \EXP{=} over \TYP{Any}, and declares \EXP{=} and
\EXP{\neq} on each integer type with an operand of that type, into which the
numeral is converted, so that there \EXP{u = 0} is \VAR{true} and
\EXP{u \neq 0} \VAR{false} for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}.
The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its
row of the revival's gap ledger: a numeral with a radix point keeps only one of
its leading zeros in its digit count, as the parser gives the numeral to both
implementations (row~960); the interpreter loads and runs a program that
writes a numeral type in a \KWD{comprises} clause (row~981); the compiled path keeps a numeral's own type,
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}, at the selector of a

\seclabel{revival-numerals}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{types-libraries}; \secref{static-expr};
\secref{coercion}; \secref{static-arg-inference}; \secref{numeral-default};
\secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{natparams}; \secref{lib:BinaryEndianWord};
\secref{lib:BinaryLinearEndianSequence};
\secref{lib:BinaryEndianLinearEndianSequence}; \secref{revival-numeral-type};
\secref{revival-inference}; \secref{revival-asfloat};
\secref{revival-object-kinds}; \secref{revival-native-helpers}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that every numeral has a numeral type of
its own, which exists only when the program is compiled, so that no value of a
numeral type exists when the program runs: the Working Draft's
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket} for a numeral without a
radix point, and \EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket} for
one with a radix point, whose static arguments are the numeral's four numbers,
its digit count $n$, the number $m$ of its digits after the radix point, its

content.content:
Neither holds of a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter,
itself or another, or that is declared with several bounds that the interpreter
cannot meet, as it cannot meet two bounds neither of which is a subtype of the
other: such a type parameter it binds, as before, to the narrowest named common
supertype of the arguments' run-time types that the bounds permit, where there
is one, and where there is none a call that fixes a type parameter of the
second kind fails (row~591 of the revival's gap ledger).
When its dispatch chooses among declarations, it passes over a declaration with
static parameters whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes in
favour of any other declaration applicable to the call without coercion
(row~589 of the revival's gap ledger).
It fixes a type parameter by the expected type only at a reduction or a
comprehension that writes no static argument and whose value is that of a
local variable declared with a type or of a top-level or local function
declared with a return type, as the box after the list in
\secref{numeral-default} says; elsewhere it does not yet fix a type parameter
It dispatches a converted call again, except a call of an overloaded method.}

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a numeral type of its own, whose static arguments are the
numeral's four numbers, and from which \library\ define coercions to the number
types, generic over those numbers; where nothing at its place fixes a type it is
converted into its default (\secref{literals}): a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the narrower type, and an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for a numeral with a radix point.
Nothing fixes a type at a variable declared without a type; at a parameter of
type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number}, or of a type parameter declared
without a bound; at the receiver of a dotted method call whose method the
default type declares; and at a static argument that only numerals fix.
A type parameter that several numerals fix, and no other argument and no
expected type, is instantiated at the narrowest default that holds every one of
their values, an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} where any of them has a radix point, each
numeral being converted into it exactly: so for
\EXP{\VAR{pick}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T}, the call
\EXP{\VAR{pick}(3, 3000000000)} is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and the
list \EXP{\langle 3000000000, 0.5\rangle} is a
\EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{R}64\rrbracket}.
The branches of an \KWD{if} or \KWD{case} expression whose value is bound to a
variable declared without a type are read in the same way: numerals there take
the narrowest default that holds them all.
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
its default: a numeral without a radix point as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point, whose conversions into
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} tie, as an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values; and \EXP{\VAR{round}(2.50000000000000001)}, whose numeral the
declarations of \VAR{round} on \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} would leave tied, rounds the \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} nearest to
that numeral, and is 2.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 read a
numeral at its default only where its conversions tie, and only a numeral
without a radix point.

== explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md:371-446

## 11. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers 1 to 6.

1. **The split in order (variant B).** Rejected:
   - variant C, which tests `Node` first and skips 213 tests for leaves: 332 s against B's 344 s, one run
     each, within noise; its exactness needs a proof (every node class implements `Node`);
   - the JVM switch alone: 652 s, and a switch every JVM would need;
   - a class-keyed dispatch.
2. **30 cases per method.** The largest method is 4,474 bytes, against the limit of 8,000.
3. **The patch changes the generator and the file it writes, not the file alone.** A build would otherwise
   regenerate the old walker the next time `Fortress.ast` or a generator changes.
4. **An audit by branch index, not by memo hits.** The fix adds no memo.
5. **The test is in Java**, because of the scalac 2.13 limit (§8).
6. **The brief's "distance stage is `tools/count-run/`" read as `tools/distance/run.sh`.** `count-run.sh`
   runs each interpreter test under walk.

**Findings.**
- The interpreted walker (§2.2).
- The shares of the repair (+267 s) and of rung C (+109 s before the fix, +65 s after) (§3).
- After the fix, about 95 % of the component's time is in the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3).
- The checker's output depends on identity hashes (§9).
- The repair removes the distance stage's crash row and adds no site (§6).
- The other methods over the limit are negligible after the fix (§2.2).

**Defects.**
- **The interpreted walker.** My change repairs it (way 1), pinned by `WalkerJUTest`. No ledger row holds it;
  the row to write:
  - claim: the generated `Walker.walk` (`FortressAst.scala`, from `ScalaAstGenerator.java`) is 31,704 bytes
    of bytecode, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte huge-method limit, so the JVM never compiles it, and every phase
    that walks a tree runs it in the interpreter;
  - status: NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, closed by the fix's commit;
  - class: implementation gap (generator, speed);
  - spec: silent;
  - reproducer: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`;
  - found by: this probe.
- **The identity-hash dependence.** A note for row 488, with the H runs' commands and outputs (§9).

**Sentences of the specification made false:** none.

**For FACTS.**
1. **The fact.** The generated AST walker's `walk` was one method over HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit, so it ran
   interpreted. With it split in order, the count stage with row 680's repair takes 352 s instead of 911 s,
   and the distance stage 931 s instead of 2,375 s, with identical output.
   - What it means: row 680's line can land under the 690 s rule.
   - Test: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`.
   - Detail: §2.2 and §6.
2. **The fact.** The checker's output depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence, because AST hashes include
   the `Class` identity hash. One extra identity hash at start reorders the api checks and the members of
   unions in messages.
   - What it means: the stages' outputs can move with an unrelated edit (row 488).
   - Command: the driver with `-Dprobe.hashes=1`.
   - Detail: §9.
3. **The fact.** Rung C's normal form costs 12 % of the count stage before the fix, 19 % after.

case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" \
      "$D/WorldFlip.java" "$D/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
      > "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" 2>&1
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then
    echo "checker-count: javac failed; see $SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; tail -20 "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 2. run the compiler phase order through the checker over the interpreter's library under a
#    private cache
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 10 900 java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=/home/user/fortress-numeral-most-specific/tmp/rung-numeral-most-specific/jfr/count.jfr,settings=profile -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress
       -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=$OVERLOAD_CACHE \
       -cp "$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" WorldFlip -stop check "$TARGET" ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
RC=$?
# A clean check: the checker reached the component, and the run ended rc 0 with no error line.
CLEAN=

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT=/home/user/fortress-numeral-most-specific/tmp/rung-numeral-most-specific/ladder/root
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT=/home/user/fortress-numeral-most-specific/tmp/rung-numeral-most-specific/ladder
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. 104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

<!-- The specification's passages that rung N of climb batch 32 changed, each with its original and new text, the reason and the way back. -->
# Decision record: a numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it

The decision is P-46, with P-49 and P-173: at a call, a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion; among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. The Appendix I entry is `revival-numerals` (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5010`), which the three passages below belong to; no new entry was made, since the passages are that entry's own.

## 1. `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`, section "Principles of Coercion", `:111-135`

**The text before** (`:111-117` at db352c1776):

> At a call, a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its conversion into any other type is a coercion (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}). So of the declarations h(x: ZZ32) and h(x: Any), both applicable to h(5) without coercion, the call invokes the first, which is the more specific.

**The text now.** A numeral is applicable to a parameter of its default type and to one that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion. Among the declarations applicable so, where every other argument is applicable without coercion, the call invokes the most specific on the parameter types they declare (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where two are not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits. Four examples follow: `h(5)` as before; `k(5)` for `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, which invokes the first; `u = 0`; `f(1.5)` for `f(x: RR32)` beside `f(x: RR64)`, which invokes the second; and `a = 0` for `a: Any`, where the numeral takes its default.

**The callout** `\revision{revival-numerals}` of the paragraph (`:137-154`) gains the decision of 10 November 2026 and what the paragraph said until then.

**The reason.** P-46: "`u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted". Before the change the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)` took the numeral at its default and answered `false` by `SEQV` (rows 973 and 966).

**What the text fixes that the decision's words leave open.** "The most specific" is read on the declared parameter types by subtyping, the order of \secref{resolving-overloading}, between a declaration that fits the numeral at its default and one that the numeral's coercion reaches. The coercion chapter's own relation, under which `RR32` is more specific than `RR64` because it coerces to it, is not used there: it would send `f(1.5)` to `f(x: RR32)` and so change what a float numeral's default chooses, which the rung's section reserves. Both implementations are built so (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk.fss`, the assertion on `width(1.5)`).

**The way back.** Restore the two sentences above; in `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala` drop `numeralAttempt` and its call at the end of `typedApplicationOfChecked`; in `interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java` drop `belowByNumerals` and its call in `bestMatchForNumerals`; give the two walk tests their expected-failure names again.

## 2. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, entry `revival-numerals`, the Effect, `:5293-5313`

**The text before** (`:5286-5298` at db352c1776): a numeral compared by `=` with a number of a type that declares no `=` with the numeral's default type meets the top-level `=` of the libraries; the interpreter answers `u = 0` false and `u =/= 0` true for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32` (rows 966 and 973), "and whether `u = 0` is true is open"; the compiled path's own library declares `=` and `=/=` on each integer type.

**The text now.** The numeral goes to the `=` of the number's type; both implementations answer `u = 0` true and `u =/= 0` false, with the tests named; `Equality` declares `=/=` as the negation of the type's own `=`. One departure is named: the interpreter reads the rule on the value, so for `a: Any` holding a zero `NN32` it answers `a = 0` true (the new row of the gap ledger and the expected failure `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNumeralBesideAnyWalk.fss`).

**The Rationale** of the entry (`:5121-5126`) gains the decision of 10 November 2026.

**The way back.** Restore the clause; the departure's row and test go with the rule.

## 3. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, entry `revival-numeral-type`, the Effect, `:3817-3825`

**The text before** (`:3817-3825` at db352c1776): inequality was not stated in pairs: the top-level `=/=` over `Any` receives the numeral at its default, so on the interpreter `u =/= 0` is true for a zero `u` of `NN32` or `NN64`.

**The text now.** `Equality` declares `=/=` beside `=`; a numeral beside a value of a type that extends `Equality` goes to that declaration, converted into the value's type; `u =/= 0` is false and `u = 0` true.

**The reason.** The library's `Equality[\T\]` gains `opr =/=(self, other:T): Boolean = NOT (self = other)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), by the Working Draft's sentence that `e =/= e'` is `NOT (e = e')` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators", its last sentence).

**The way back.** Remove the declaration from `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and restore the sentence.

## The front matter

`Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`'s paragraph on the revision is not made false: it names no rule of a numeral at a call.
EOF

# Decision record: a numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration that takes it

The decision is P-46, with P-49 and P-173: at a call, a numeral is applicable to a parameter that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion; among the applicable declarations the most specific runs, and where two are not ordered, the one that the default fits. The Appendix I entry is `revival-numerals` (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5010`), which the three passages below belong to; no new entry was made, since the passages are that entry's own.

## 1. `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`, section "Principles of Coercion", `:111-135`

**The text before** (`:111-117` at db352c1776):

> At a call, a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its conversion into any other type is a coercion (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}). So of the declarations h(x: ZZ32) and h(x: Any), both applicable to h(5) without coercion, the call invokes the first, which is the more specific.

**The text now.** A numeral is applicable to a parameter of its default type and to one that fixes no type, at its default, and to a parameter whose type declares a coercion from the numeral's type, by that coercion. Among the declarations applicable so, where every other argument is applicable without coercion, the call invokes the most specific on the parameter types they declare (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where two are not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits. Four examples follow: `h(5)` as before; `k(5)` for `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, which invokes the first; `u = 0`; `f(1.5)` for `f(x: RR32)` beside `f(x: RR64)`, which invokes the second; and `a = 0` for `a: Any`, where the numeral takes its default.

**The callout** `\revision{revival-numerals}` of the paragraph (`:137-154`) gains the decision of 10 November 2026 and what the paragraph said until then.

**The reason.** P-46: "`u = 0` is `true` for `u: NN32 = 0`, and no way that answers `false` is accepted". Before the change the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)` took the numeral at its default and answered `false` by `SEQV` (rows 973 and 966).

**What the text fixes that the decision's words leave open.** "The most specific" is read on the declared parameter types by subtyping, the order of \secref{resolving-overloading}, between a declaration that fits the numeral at its default and one that the numeral's coercion reaches. The coercion chapter's own relation, under which `RR32` is more specific than `RR64` because it coerces to it, is not used there: it would send `f(1.5)` to `f(x: RR32)` and so change what a float numeral's default chooses, which the rung's section reserves. Both implementations are built so (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk.fss`, the assertion on `width(1.5)`).

**The way back.** Restore the two sentences above; in `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala` drop `numeralAttempt` and its call at the end of `typedApplicationOfChecked`; in `interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java` drop `belowByNumerals` and its call in `bestMatchForNumerals`; give the two walk tests their expected-failure names again.

## 2. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, entry `revival-numerals`, the Effect, `:5293-5313`

**The text before** (`:5286-5298` at db352c1776): a numeral compared by `=` with a number of a type that declares no `=` with the numeral's default type meets the top-level `=` of the libraries; the interpreter answers `u = 0` false and `u =/= 0` true for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32` (rows 966 and 973), "and whether `u = 0` is true is open"; the compiled path's own library declares `=` and `=/=` on each integer type.

**The text now.** The numeral goes to the `=` of the number's type; both implementations answer `u = 0` true and `u =/= 0` false, with the tests named; `Equality` declares `=/=` as the negation of the type's own `=`. One departure is named: the interpreter reads the rule on the value, so for `a: Any` holding a zero `NN32` it answers `a = 0` true (the new row of the gap ledger and the expected failure `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNumeralBesideAnyWalk.fss`).

**The Rationale** of the entry (`:5121-5126`) gains the decision of 10 November 2026.

**The way back.** Restore the clause; the departure's row and test go with the rule.

## 3. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, entry `revival-numeral-type`, the Effect, `:3817-3825`

**The text before** (`:3817-3825` at db352c1776): inequality was not stated in pairs: the top-level `=/=` over `Any` receives the numeral at its default, so on the interpreter `u =/= 0` is true for a zero `u` of `NN32` or `NN64`.

**The text now.** `Equality` declares `=/=` beside `=`; a numeral beside a value of a type that extends `Equality` goes to that declaration, converted into the value's type; `u =/= 0` is false and `u = 0` true.

**The reason.** The library's `Equality[\T\]` gains `opr =/=(self, other:T): Boolean = NOT (self = other)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), by the Working Draft's sentence that `e =/= e'` is `NOT (e = e')` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators", its last sentence).

**The way back.** Remove the declaration from `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and restore the sentence.

## The front matter

`Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`'s paragraph on the revision is not made false: it names no rule of a numeral at a call.
